event: Built by Meyer Werft, Papenburg (West Germany) as Viking Sally for Rederi Ab Sally (Viking Line traffic).
Sailed as Silja Star and then Wasa King before sale to Estline, a joint venture of the Estonian state and Swedish company Nordström & Thulin; renamed Estonia in 1993 for the Tallinn–Stockholm route.
Swedish Armed Forces ship non-explosive military electronic equipment aboard Estonia, as later confirmed by the 2005 Hirschfeldt inquiry.
Estonia departs Tallinn for Stockholm with 989 people aboard (803 passengers, 186 crew), fully loaded with vehicles. Weather deteriorates during the evening.
Heavy metallic bangs from the bow are heard by crew and passengers. A seaman on the car deck reports the noise to the bridge.
Per JAIC, the bow visor separates and the bow ramp is pulled open; water floods the car deck and the ship rapidly takes a heavy starboard list.
First Mayday transmitted. It does not follow the standard format and the position is given only later, delaying the wider response.
Estonia disappears from radar screens and sinks stern-first in international waters (Finnish search and rescue region) south of the island of Utö, coming to rest at roughly 70–85 m depth.
Viking Line ferry Mariella is the first ship on scene, followed by Silja Europa, Silja Symphony, Isabella and others. Large ferries struggle to recover people from rafts in the heavy sea.
Finnish and Swedish helicopters begin winching survivors from rafts and the water. In total 138 people are rescued, one of whom later dies in hospital.
The bow visor is located on the seabed about a nautical mile west of the wreck and later raised for examination.

Estonia, Finland and Sweden sign the Estonia Agreement declaring the wreck a final place of rest and banning disturbance. Other countries later accede. Plans to entomb the wreck are eventually abandoned.
JAIC publishes its final report: visor lock failure under wave loads, inadequate design, and criticism of the crew's speed and the emergency response.
Gregg Bemis and Jutta Rabe dive to the wreck despite the ban; the German Group of Experts report disputes JAIC.
Former Stockholm customs chief Lennart Henriksson reveals military cargo on earlier crossings. The Hirschfeldt inquiry confirms 14 & 20 September shipments but none on the fatal night.
Estonian government expert committee led by Margus Kurm criticises the JAIC report's handling of survivor testimony.
SSPA and HSVA consortia present sinking-sequence studies: broadly consistent with JAIC, but the sinking began earlier than JAIC stated.
Discovery documentary reveals a ~4 m × 1.2 m breach in the starboard hull. Governments announce a new examination.
Official seabed and wreck surveys by the Estonian, Swedish and Finnish authorities. Filmmakers Evertsson and Andersson are convicted on retrial of violating the grave peace.
The 12-tonne bow ramp is raised from the seabed and taken to Estonia for examination.
Joint final report of the Preliminary Assessment: the ship sank due to failure of the bow structure; the starboard damage came from seabed contact; no reopening of the safety investigation.
